transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-03
Time: 17:00 UTC (09:00 PT)
Duration: 47 min
Title: Helix Pharma - Procurement/Legal + Security Sync (NDA, SOC 2, Subprocessors, Security Addendum)
Organizer: Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood Inference)
Attendees (Redwood): Stephanie Nguyen (Sales), Olga Petrov (GRC), Michael Grant (Legal), Fatima Noor (Solutions Engineering)
Attendees (Helix Pharma): Dana Whitaker (Procurement), Raj Patel (Legal), Mina Al-Karim (InfoSec), Evan Brooks (IT Infra)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Helix requests Redwood SOC 2 Type II report under NDA and clarifies evidence-sharing process.
- Legal and Security review key terms: breach notification timing, audit rights, subprocessor disclosures, data retention/deletion language, and security addendum scope.
- Redwood confirms standard approach: SOC 2 report is shared under NDA via evidence request workflow; subprocessor list can be provided; breach notification commitments are contract-dependent and reviewed case-by-case.
- Discussed differences between Hosted/Dedicated vs Private deployments and shared responsibility boundaries.

Topics
1) NDA required for SOC 2 report + evidence request workflow
2) Subprocessor list and notification expectations
3) Breach notification window and incident response comms
4) Audit rights / security questionnaires / onsite assessment language
5) Data retention and deletion language alignment (logs vs prompts)
6) Private/VPC deployment responsibility split and access controls

Questions captured
- Can Redwood provide SOC 2 Type II report and latest bridge letter under NDA?
- Does Redwood use customer prompts/outputs to train models? (definition + exceptions)
- How does Redwood notify on new subprocessors and what is the objection process?
- What breach notification time window can Redwood commit to (24/48/72 hours)?
- Can Helix perform an audit / penetration test of the environment?
- Where can data be processed for EU sites, and is data residency guaranteed for Hosted vs Private?

Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, I think we’re good. Hi everyone—thanks for making time. The goal today is pretty narrow: get aligned on NDA for SOC 2 access, and then walk through the redline themes you all flagged—subprocessors, breach notice, and the security addendum.

[00:16] Dana Whitaker: Yep, thanks Stephanie. We’re trying to avoid a long back-and-forth. If we can agree the process today, we can keep procurement moving.

[00:23] Mina Al-Karim: And for security, we just need the SOC 2 Type II, the scope, and any exceptions. We’ve got internal governance, so I need something I can attach to our risk ticket.

[00:33] Raj Patel: Plus the contract language. The addendum our team uses has specific breach notification and audit rights clauses.

[00:40] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense. Quick intros on our side: Olga is our GRC lead, Michael is legal, and Fatima is solutions engineering—she’s been supporting the Private deployment questions.

[00:51] Olga Petrov: Hi everyone.

[00:53] Michael Grant: Morning.

[00:55] Fatima Noor: Hi.

[00:58] Evan Brooks: Hey, Evan here. I’m mostly listening, but if the conversation goes into VPC, networking, whatever, I’ll jump in.

[01:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Olga, can you start with SOC 2 and NDA requirements?

[01:11] Olga Petrov: Sure. We can provide the SOC 2 Type II report under NDA. We use an evidence request workflow—basically it’s tracked, and we share through a gated link. If you already have a mutual NDA with Redwood, we can use that; otherwise we can execute one quickly. We generally don’t email the full report as an attachment.

[01:31] Dana Whitaker: We have our own NDA template. Does Redwood accept customer paper or do you require your own?

[01:37] Michael Grant: We can review your template. In many cases we can accept it with minimal changes, but we do need a few specifics—confidentiality definition, permitted recipients, and no “public filing” style carve-outs. If you send it today, we can turn it quickly.

[01:52] Raj Patel: Our template is pretty standard. The sticking point has been “residuals” clauses with some vendors—does Redwood include that?

[01:59] Michael Grant: We generally avoid residuals for security audit artifacts. If your NDA has a residuals provision, we’ll likely propose removing it for confidential security materials.

[02:09] Raj Patel: Okay.

[02:10] Mina Al-Karim: For the SOC 2 specifically—Type II, what period and which system? We’ve had vendors send a SOC 2 for like HR systems and call it a day.

[02:20] Olga Petrov: Totally fair. The report covers the in-scope production systems supporting our inference platform—control plane services, logging, access control processes, incident response, that type of thing. The exact scope statement is in the report. Once NDA is executed, I can provide the full report plus the auditor’s opinion and any exceptions.

[02:40] Mina Al-Karim: And a bridge letter if the report period ended last quarter?

[02:44] Olga Petrov: If applicable, yes—we can provide a bridge letter under NDA, subject to availability and timing.

[02:50] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Next: subprocessors. Mina, do you want to frame what you need?

[02:56] Mina Al-Karim: Yes. We need a list of subprocessors that could touch data—support tooling, infrastructure providers, logging, etc. And we need to know the notification process when the list changes. Our DPA requires notice and the right to object.

[03:11] Fatima Noor: I can speak at a high level and then Olga/Michael can cover contractual. By deployment mode: for Hosted and Dedicated, we operate the platform on major cloud infrastructure—so cloud provider is a subprocessor. For Private deployments, the customer controls more of that boundary, depending on whether it’s in your VPC or on-prem.

[03:30] Evan Brooks: When you say “Private in our VPC,” does Redwood still have access? Like are you managing it as a service, or is it a software install?

[03:38] Fatima Noor: It’s a managed deployment with a private control plane integration—customer-managed networking, and Redwood has limited administrative access as defined contractually and technically. We can go deeper in the follow-up. But in that model, you still may have subprocessors for support ticketing and some operational tooling, depending on what you enable.

[03:58] Mina Al-Karim: Right. So we need the canonical list.

[04:02] Olga Petrov: We can provide the current subprocessor list under NDA, and we also have a standard notification mechanism—email notice with a defined window. The exact window can be negotiated in the DPA, but we try to keep it consistent.

[04:17] Raj Patel: Our standard is 30 days prior notice, and right to terminate if we reasonably object.

[04:23] Michael Grant: That’s a common construct. We’ll need to look at the exact language—especially around “terminate for convenience” versus termination limited to the impacted service. But yes, we can work from that.

[04:37] Dana Whitaker: Is the subprocessor list public? Some vendors publish it.

[04:41] Olga Petrov: We don’t keep it fully public because it can be sensitive and changes. But we can share the list and the process under NDA.

[04:49] Mina Al-Karim: Okay. Also—do you use customer prompts or outputs to train models? We need a clear statement.

[04:56] Stephanie Nguyen: We get that question a lot. Olga, do you want to give the approved wording?

[05:01] Olga Petrov: Sure. Redwood does not use customer content—prompts or outputs—to train our base models. For operational purposes, some metadata and logs may be retained per configuration and policy, but not used for training. If there are any optional features that would involve customer-provided datasets for fine-tuning, that would be explicitly contracted and opt-in.

[05:22] Mina Al-Karim: Good. We’ll want that in writing in the questionnaire response.

[05:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, we’ll include the approved phrasing in the recap.

[05:31] Raj Patel: Moving to breach notification. Our security addendum says: “Vendor shall notify within 24 hours of discovery of a Security Incident.” Can Redwood do that?

[05:42] Michael Grant: We can commit to prompt notification, but 24 hours from discovery is sometimes challenging depending on what “incident” is defined as. We typically align to a standard like without undue delay and within a specified outer bound for confirmed incidents involving customer data. Often customers ask for 72 hours, sometimes 48.

[06:06] Raj Patel: Our policy is 24. It’s not always a hard requirement, but we need a business justification if we accept 72.

[06:14] Mina Al-Karim: From security perspective, 24 is ideal, but I’m also realistic. What I don’t want is “at your discretion.”

[06:22] Michael Grant: Understood. What I can do is take your exact definition of “Security Incident,” and propose an approach: (1) notify within 24 hours for confirmed incidents impacting Helix data in scope, and (2) for suspected incidents, provide an initial notice as soon as practical with follow-up as facts are confirmed. But I can’t promise final wording until I see the addendum.

[06:47] Raj Patel: That’s the right direction.

[06:50] Stephanie Nguyen: And operationally, we do have an on-call and incident process. The nuance is mostly legal definitions.

[06:56] Mina Al-Karim: Do you have a standard incident response plan you can share?

[07:00] Olga Petrov: We don’t typically share the full IR plan, but we can provide a summary and confirm key elements—roles, severity, communication path—under NDA as part of the evidence package.

[07:10] Mina Al-Karim: Okay.

[07:12] Raj Patel: Next: audit rights. Our addendum includes a right to audit vendor facilities and systems, including penetration testing, on reasonable notice.

[07:22] Michael Grant: That’s an area where we have to be careful. We generally provide third-party audit reports like SOC 2 and sometimes allow reasonable security questionnaires. We don’t allow customer-initiated penetration testing of our multi-tenant production environment. For Private deployments, there may be more flexibility depending on scope and rules of engagement, but it needs to be controlled.

[07:43] Evan Brooks: If it’s in our VPC, can we scan it like we scan our own stuff?

[07:48] Fatima Noor: In a VPC deployment, you would typically have more ability to run vulnerability scans on the network and endpoints you control. But there may still be components Redwood manages and we’d need to coordinate to avoid disruption. Usually we define permitted testing in a policy.

[08:07] Mina Al-Karim: That’s fine. We just need to know it’s not a black box. SOC 2 helps, but for regulated systems we often do some validation.

[08:16] Michael Grant: That’s a common compromise: rely on SOC 2 plus a controlled mechanism for additional assurance—like sharing pen test executive summaries or allowing customer review under supervision.

[08:29] Raj Patel: Our template language is pretty blunt. We can consider an alternative if you propose something concrete.

[08:35] Michael Grant: Will do.

[08:37] Stephanie Nguyen: On retention and deletion—this came up in your email as well. Mina, what’s your requirement?

[08:44] Mina Al-Karim: We need clarity on what you store and for how long. Specifically: prompts, outputs, embeddings, logs, and audit logs. Some vendors say “we don’t store” but then keep everything in logs.

[08:58] Olga Petrov: Great point. The correct way to say it is: behavior depends on deployment mode and configuration. In Hosted, there are operational logs; in Dedicated and Private, we have more configurability and isolation. We can provide our customer-facing retention/deletion overview—again, we want to avoid overpromising. Certain logs are retained for security and operational reliability, but there are controls and defined retention windows.

[09:22] Mina Al-Karim: Can we set it to zero retention for prompts and outputs?

[09:27] Fatima Noor: For some workloads, yes, we can minimize retention, but “zero” has caveats—like transient processing and the need to keep minimal metadata for billing and abuse prevention. It also depends on streaming and debugging settings.

[09:41] Mina Al-Karim: Understood. Just want it spelled out.

[09:45] Raj Patel: Our DPA also requires deletion within X days after termination.

[09:50] Michael Grant: We can address that in the DPA. Typically we commit to delete customer data within a defined period after termination, subject to legal retention requirements and backup cycles, and we separate that from security logs.

[10:08] Dana Whitaker: Okay. Can I pause—are we aligned that SOC 2 report is gated until NDA is signed, and you’ll review our NDA quickly?

[10:16] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. If you send it today, we’ll prioritize.

[10:19] Dana Whitaker: Good.

[10:21] (crosstalk)

[10:22] Mina Al-Karim: One more—subprocessors by region. We have EU sites. Can we guarantee EU processing?

[10:29] Fatima Noor: For Private deployments in your VPC in the EU, you’d have strong residency control because the workload runs where you deploy it. For Hosted, we can talk about region availability, but we need to be careful—some operational services could still be global. We don’t want to state absolute residency unless the specific architecture and contract supports it.

[10:52] Mina Al-Karim: That’s what I need to know: what’s guaranteed vs “best effort.”

[10:57] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll set up a separate residency/data flow session. Today we’ll keep it on legal/security artifacts.

[11:04] Raj Patel: Okay. Another clause: breach cooperation and costs. Our addendum pushes all costs to vendor.

[11:10] Michael Grant: We’ll need to evaluate. Typically, each party bears its own costs, with vendor bearing costs for remediation under its control. If you have a hard stance, we can escalate, but it’s not always accepted as-is.

[11:25] Raj Patel: Understood. We’ll list as a discussion point.

[11:29] Olga Petrov: On the evidence package—beyond SOC 2, what else do you need? Some customers ask for policies, vulnerability scan reports, pen tests.

[11:38] Mina Al-Karim: Minimum: SOC 2 Type II, subprocessor list, security FAQ, and a high-level architecture/data flow description. If we can get pen test results, even a summary, that helps.

[11:52] Olga Petrov: Noted. We can share an executive summary where available under NDA. Full detailed findings are usually restricted.

[12:01] Mina Al-Karim: That’s okay.

[12:03] Evan Brooks: On access controls: if we go Private, can we integrate SSO and have RBAC? We need least privilege.

[12:11] Fatima Noor: Yes—SSO/SAML for console access, SCIM in many cases, and role-based access control. Audit logs are available—again, depends on plan and deployment, but it’s a core requirement for enterprise.

[12:24] Mina Al-Karim: And audit log export? We use Splunk.

[12:28] Fatima Noor: There are export options—SIEM and storage destinations—though I don’t want to overstate specifics without checking your preferred method. We can follow up with the doc link and what’s currently supported.

[12:44] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll capture that and respond with the approved doc references.

[12:48] Raj Patel: Great. So process-wise: we’ll send NDA template and our addendum. You’ll come back with a redline and evidence package once NDA is signed.

[12:58] Michael Grant: Correct.

[13:00] Olga Petrov: Correct.

[13:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Before we wrap, anything else blocking procurement?

[13:06] Dana Whitaker: Timeline. We’re aiming to submit vendor packet by end of next week. If the NDA and SOC 2 slip, it delays.

[13:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We can turn NDA review in 1–2 business days if it’s standard.

[13:21] Raj Patel: And the breach notification stance—if you can propose something close to 24 hours, that will help.

[13:27] Michael Grant: I’ll prioritize that section.

[13:29] Mina Al-Karim: Also make sure the “no training on customer data” statement is explicit.

[13:34] Olga Petrov: Yep.

[13:35] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. I’m going to do a quick recap of next steps.

[13:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Dana and Raj: send NDA template and security addendum/DPA redlines by Thursday. Olga: prep SOC 2 access steps and evidence list; share once NDA is in place. Michael: draft initial redline positions on breach notice, audit rights, and subprocessor notice/objection. Fatima: send subprocessor overview and a short note on shared responsibility for Hosted vs Private. And I’ll book a follow-up to go deep on data flows/residency.

[14:12] Dana Whitaker: Sounds good.

[14:14] Raj Patel: Works.

[14:15] Mina Al-Karim: Thanks.

[14:17] Evan Brooks: Thanks everyone.

[14:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great—appreciate it. Talk soon.

(Recording ends; remainder of transcript not captured due to early stop / Fireflies disconnect)
